b: “People only raise their voices when they feel like they aren’t being heard,” Nicholas Hoult’s Ryan, a bank robber turned viral video star, suggests in a confessional video in How to Rob a Bank. There’s no shortage of such primal wails against the dehumanizing machinery of contemporary capitalism in David Leitch’s action thriller. But Leitch and screenwriter Mark Bianculli too often mistake a loud voice for a profound one, rendering their attempts at political relevance as toothless as a mean tweet.

The film, which takes its name from the YouTube series that Ryan and his clout-chasing crew use to document their Robin Hood-inspired exploits, has a satirical bent. The gang’s slickly produced explainer videos strike a nerve in the public consciousness by fusing the anti-corporate wrath of a Luigi Mangione with all the goofy gamification of a MrBeast. These rapid-fire montages provide the lone spark of energy in How to Rob a Bank, if only because they demonstrate some thoughtfulness in dismantling common heist-movie clichés.

Bianculli’s script never effectively channels the populist fury of those seeking to turn the financial system upside down. Until a mid-movie exposition dump, the robbers are nothing but lawless mouthpieces of redistributive rage. And even once some details about their personalities arrive, Bianculli never develops them as anything more than the sum of their radicalizing traumas. A litany of obstacles to social mobility for young Americans—medical debt, student loans, the neglect of forever-war veterans—is meant to serve as a substitute for characterization.

Their adversaries on the other side of the law don’t fare much better. Old-school FBI investigator John West (John C. Reilly) knows he has no hope of identifying the tech-savvy bandits during their reign of robbery over Pittsburgh’s banks. In an act of desperation, he brings on a nihilistic coder, Reagan Gardner (Zoë Kravitz), to pinpoint the group’s location and stop them from sticking up the last major target in town. Reilly and Kravitz’s intentional lack of chemistry never settles into the kind of odd-couple routine that the film is aiming for, and the awkward pacing of their exchanges feels especially leaden next to the zippily edited robberies.

Like many a cinematic stick-up, How to Rob a Bank falls apart less because of flaws in its grand design than because of small errors. Leitch’s film squanders the magnetism and soulfulness of Hoult’s emotive face by sticking him under a wolf mask for most of its key sequences. The piercing gaze of his saucer eyes, Tom Cruise-like in its intensity, still peeks out from underneath Ryan’s lupine disguise. But those eyes can only do so much when the script gives Hoult so little to work with; stripped of any meaningful backstory, his bleach-blond baddie mostly just broods.

Leitch, who spent years as a stunt performer and coordinator before becoming a director, also never gets to use his full skill set. Apart from one impressive vehicle flip during a car chase, How to Rob a Bank lacks a single standout action set piece. At least other studio films that make empty gestures at topicality have the decency to provide some shallow entertainment value.

“Let’s make some content!” the marauders proclaim before their first holdup. How to Rob a Bank follows their lead, though it’s modeled on the most obvious attributes of social media content: the sugar rush of scroll-stopping hooks, the formulaic storytelling, and the hollow engagement bait that prioritizes quippy sloganeering over real substance. Viewers hoping for truth in advertising from the title are bound to come away disappointed, though they’ll still get a lesson of sorts: not in how to rob a bank, but in how not to make a heist film.
